title: Market orders

inOneLine.simple: A market order opens a trade now, at the best price available. You buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[market-order]] trades immediately: buys fill near the [[ask]], sells near the [[bid]]. Speed is certain; the exact price is not.

explain.simple: A market order says: open my trade now. A buy fills at the ask, the higher price. A sell fills at the bid, the lower price. To close, you do the opposite: a buy is closed by selling at the bid, and a sell is closed by buying at the ask. That is why a new trade shows a small loss straight away. It is the spread.
explain.balanced: Market orders favour speed over price. The fill can differ from the price on screen if the market moves while the order travels, which is called [[slippage]]. Profit or loss on a buy = (closing bid − opening ask) in pips × [[pip-value]]. On a sell = (opening bid − closing ask) in pips × pip value.

assumptions: Buy 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR; pip value 1 USD
steps: The buy fills at the ask: 1.10012.
To close now you would sell at the bid: 1.10000.
Open result right away = −1.2 × 1 USD = −1.20 USD. That is the spread cost.

assumptions: Sell 0.10 lot GBP/USD = 10,000 GBP; pip value 1 USD
steps: The sell fills at the bid: 1.25000.
To close, you buy at the ask: 1.24820.

explainSimpler: A market order is like saying 'I'll take it at whatever the price is now.' You get in fast, but you start a little behind because of the spread.
commonMistake: Working out a sell trade's result from the bid on the chart. A sell closes at the ask, which is higher than the bid by the spread, so the real result is a bit worse than the chart line suggests.

quickCheck.prompt: You have an open buy trade. At which price will it close?

options.explanation: Right: closing a buy means selling, and sells happen at the bid.
No: the ask is where a buy opens, not where it closes.

options.text: The price where you opened the trade
options.explanation: No: the price has moved since then. A buy closes at the current bid.

quickCheck.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD (pip value 1 USD) at ask 1.10050. You close at bid 1.10350. What is the result?

options.explanation: No: 0.00300 is 30 pips, and 30 × 1 USD = 30 USD. 300 USD would need a pip value of 10 USD (1 lot).
No: you bought and the price rose, so this is a profit.

doItNow.instructions: Open the P/L calculator. Enter the GBP/USD sell from the second example and check you get the same answer. Then try a buy that loses 25 pips at 0.10 lot.

homework: On your demo account, open a 0.01 lot market buy on EUR/USD and note the price it filled at and the result shown straight away. Close it and note the closing price.
